title: Leg ulcer examination

header.contentArea: Clinical examination / vascular and wound assessment
guidelineVersions: NWCSP Lower Limb Recommendations for Clinical Care (2023)

brief.scenario: You are the core surgical trainee in a vascular assessment clinic.
brief.task: Examine the lower legs of a 69-year-old patient with a right lower-leg ulcer. Explain your findings to the examiner, distinguish likely venous from arterial or neuropathic causes, and outline safe initial investigation and management. Use the examination model/patient and request any unavailable findings from the examiner. Do not remove dressings without permission.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: This is a vascular examination with an ulcer, not merely a wound description. Establish arterial safety before recommending therapeutic compression.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Attributing every gaiter ulcer to venous disease without testing arterial perfusion.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: “I’ll inspect both legs, examine arterial pulses and sensation, and assess the ulcer before deciding on compression.”

flow: 0–1 min: introduce, consent, pain control, exposure and position
1–3 min: compare skin, oedema, venous changes, ulcer dimensions and bed
3–5 min: examine both limbs for temperature, capillary refill, pulses and neuropathy
5–7 min: synthesise likely venous ulcer plus possible mixed arterial disease; request ABPI/Doppler if needed
7–9 min: recommend dressing, measured vascular assessment, compression only when safe, red-flag escalation and referral

grid.label: Introduction and comfort
grid.borderline: Consent given but poor positioning or pain assessment
grid.pass: Introduces self, gains consent, asks pain and adjusts exposure
grid.high: Explains each manoeuvre and avoids wound trauma

grid.label: Bilateral inspection
grid.fail: Looks at ulcer alone, ignores other leg
grid.borderline: Notes ulcer but omits venous skin changes
grid.pass: Compares both legs for oedema, varicosities, pigmentation, eczema and scars
grid.high: Connects distribution of oedema and gaiter skin changes to venous hypertension

grid.label: Ulcer characterisation
grid.pass: States site, dimensions, edge, bed, exudate, periwound skin and infection signs
grid.high: Distinguishes clinically infected tissue from colonisation and documents monitoring baseline

grid.label: Arterial supply
grid.fail: Recommends strong compression without any arterial assessment
grid.borderline: Feels only one pulse without interpreting significance
grid.pass: Checks temperature, refill, dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial pulses bilaterally; requests Doppler/ABPI
grid.high: Recognises palpable pulses do not exclude peripheral arterial disease; considers toe pressures when ABPI is unreliable

grid.label: Neuropathy and other causes
grid.pass: Assesses protective sensation and pressure/trauma patterns
grid.high: Considers vasculitis, malignancy and atypical ulcer red flags if presentation does not fit

grid.label: Clinical interpretation
grid.fail: Calls it definitely venous and safe for compression
grid.borderline: Suggests venous cause but misses possible mixed disease
grid.pass: States probable venous ulcer, arterial status not yet established
grid.high: Explains mixed aetiology risk and diagnostic limits of bedside examination

grid.label: Compression safety
grid.fail: Starts strong compression without establishing arterial adequacy
grid.borderline: Defers decision but offers no plan
grid.pass: Requests reliable arterial assessment before full compression; no strong compression if significant ischaemia suspected
grid.high: Uses specialist pathway for mixed disease and cautions about falsely high ABPI in calcified vessels

grid.label: Referral and monitoring
grid.pass: Documents ulcer, arranges wound review and vascular referral for venous ulcer
grid.high: Recommends duplex to define reflux and supports multidisciplinary care

grid.label: Safety and escalation
grid.fail: Misses cold painful foot and sepsis
grid.borderline: Recognises red flag but delays response
grid.pass: Urgently escalates acute limb ischaemia, spreading infection or systemic illness
grid.high: States immediate priorities and tells patient when urgent return is needed

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I need to look at your ulcer. Let me lift the dressing now.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: That pulls on the sore skin.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It is on the ankle and looks superficial. I think it is venous.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Would you examine the rest of the leg?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The swollen ankle is enough to know. I do not need the other leg.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: One pulse is probably there, so arterial disease is excluded.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The posterior tibial pulse is faint; there is no ABPI available.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I would apply full-strength compression immediately anyway.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: This is definitely a venous ulcer, so compression is safe.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Could anything else be contributing to this ulcer?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No. I would not check sensation or ask about diabetes or pressure; leg ulcers are either venous or arterial.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: A dressing each week is adequate. No specialist referral is needed.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The patient asks what to do if the foot becomes cold and suddenly very painful.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Leave it until next week; cold feet happen.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: That worries me because it could get worse.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: There is nothing urgent to check.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I’m the core surgical trainee. I’d like to examine your legs and the ulcer. Is that all right? Is it sore if I touch near it?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: That’s fine. The skin is tender close to the dressing, not terribly painful.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will keep the wound protected and uncover only what is necessary. Please tell me if I hurt you.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: With both legs exposed appropriately, I can see swelling around the ankles and brown skin staining, with visible superficial veins. I will compare the opposite limb.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The pigmentation is bilateral; oedema is worse on the right.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: May I inspect the ulcer and surrounding skin without scraping its bed?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: It is 3 by 2 centimetres at the right medial gaiter region, shallow with granulation, an irregular sloping edge and moderate serous exudate.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would record its site, size, bed, edge, discharge and surrounding skin. Is there spreading erythema, pus, malodour or fever?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: None. The patient is systemically well.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I am assessing the arterial supply before planning compression. I will check foot warmth, capillary refill and both pedal pulses on each side.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Both feet are warm. Right posterior tibial pulse is faint; dorsalis pedis is palpable. Capillary refill is approximately two seconds.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Palpable pulses do not reliably exclude arterial disease. I would arrange Doppler ABPI and assess whether toe pressures are required if ABPI seems unreliable.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Do you have diabetes or loss of sensation in your feet? I will check protective sensation with a suitable monofilament and look for pressure points.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: I do not have diabetes and have not noticed numbness.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Protective sensation is preserved and there are no obvious pressure lesions.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The location, oedema, skin staining and varicosities suggest a venous ulcer. But I cannot confirm adequate arterial perfusion from inspection and pulses alone.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What would you do next?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would arrange formal arterial assessment before prescribing full therapeutic compression. If there is clinically important arterial disease, compression needs specialist assessment rather than routine application.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would document a wound baseline, use an appropriate non-adherent dressing and arrange trained wound-care review, venous duplex and vascular referral.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Suppose the patient says their foot suddenly becomes cold and severely painful tonight.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That is an emergency suggesting acute limb ischaemia. They need immediate emergency assessment, not routine clinic follow-up. I would arrange urgent vascular escalation.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Please seek urgent help also for fever, rapidly spreading redness or feeling acutely unwell. Do you have any questions?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: No, I understand why you need the circulation test first.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Good morning. I’m one of the core surgical trainees. I understand you have a leg wound that is slow to heal. Before I inspect it, is it painful today, and would you prefer a short pause if it becomes uncomfortable?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: It is more itchy than painful.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Thank you. I’ll examine both legs, because the comparison helps identify the underlying circulation problem. May I proceed?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Yes.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I’m comparing both limbs from the knees to the toes: asymmetry, swelling, varicose veins, scars, pigment change, eczema and skin thickening. The medial ankle location with pigmentation and oedema suggests long-standing venous pressure.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The right ankle is more oedematous; there is bilateral haemosiderin staining.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would gently expose the ulcer, measure it and record its depth, margins, granulation, exudate and periwound changes. Are there signs of local infection or a necrotic base?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: It measures 3 × 2 cm, is superficial and granulating, with moderate serous exudate. There is no spreading erythema or necrosis.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would not equate a colonised wound with clinical infection. I would photograph it only with appropriate consent and documentation to compare healing.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Now arterial assessment: temperature and colour of both feet, refill, femoral and distal pulses as appropriate, particularly dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial. I will not infer arterial sufficiency just from one palpable pulse.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The feet are warm, the right posterior tibial pulse is faint and the dorsalis pedis is present.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will also test protective sensation and look for deformity or pressure injury. Can you tell me about diabetes, smoking, calf pain on walking or pain at night relieved by hanging the foot down?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: No diabetes and no night pain. My ankle swells by evening.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Protective sensation is normal.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: This is most consistent with a venous gaiter ulcer, possibly mixed with arterial disease. The right posterior tibial finding is a reason to document formal vascular testing rather than declare compression safe.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Can we apply a high-strength compression bandage today?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Not before arterial adequacy is established through validated testing. I would obtain a Doppler ABPI, consider toe pressure if vessels are non-compressible, and follow the local specialist pathway. Reduced compression may be considered by an experienced service in selected mixed disease; that is not a blanket instruction. If there are no red flags, mild graduated compression of 20 mmHg or less at the ankle can be started while we wait; strong compression should be considered only once the ABPI is above 0.8.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What will you arrange for the vein problem?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would refer the active venous ulcer to the vascular service and seek duplex assessment for treatable superficial reflux. Meanwhile I would coordinate wound measurement, suitable simple dressing, ankle mobility and follow-up.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: At the end, the patient asks: “What if the whole foot turns icy cold and hurts suddenly?”

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That changes the urgency completely. Sudden severe pain and a cold foot require emergency vascular assessment the same day, immediately if acute limb ischaemia is suspected; I would not ask them to wait for ABPI at clinic.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would also give clear infection precautions and check the patient can contact the service. Could you tell me what would make you seek urgent help?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: A suddenly cold, painful foot, fever, or fast-spreading redness.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Exactly. The key is to treat the cause of the ulcer while ensuring the circulation is safe for treatment.

failures.move: Applies strong compression without assessing arterial sufficiency.
failures.consequence: May worsen critical limb ischaemia in mixed arterial disease.

failures.move: Tells the patient to delay assessment of a sudden cold painful foot.
failures.consequence: Could miss acute limb ischaemia and limb loss.

failures.move: Ignores spreading infection or systemic illness.
failures.consequence: May delay treatment of severe soft-tissue infection or sepsis.

recovery.when: If you implied a palpable pulse makes full compression safe
recovery.line: I need to correct that: a palpable pulse does not establish that full compression is safe. I will request formal arterial assessment.

recovery.when: If a newly cold and painful foot is described
recovery.line: A newly cold and painful foot would change this to an emergency; I would arrange immediate vascular assessment.

knowledge.fact: Medial gaiter ulcers with oedema and haemosiderin often suggest venous disease; morphology alone is not proof.
Wound size and wound-bed status form the baseline for judging healing; wound imaging is standard practice, and ankle circumference should be measured at every visit.

Palpation of peripheral pulses is an unreliable form of arterial assessment; pair it with handheld Doppler ABPI, and consider toe pressures where ABPI is unreliable (for example medial arterial calcification in diabetes or kidney disease).

Without red flags, mild graduated compression (20 mmHg or less at the ankle) can be offered at first presentation, with full assessment within 14 days. Consider strong compression only if ABPI is above 0.8; ABPI below 0.5 indicates chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and needs urgent vascular referral.
An active or healed venous leg ulcer is an indication for vascular service referral.
Acute or suspected chronic limb-threatening ischaemia, acute infection and symptoms of sepsis are red flags requiring immediate escalation to the relevant specialist.

recall.think: venous-pattern ulcer, but exclude significant arterial disease.
recall.say: “The ulcer looks venous, but I must establish perfusion before full compression.”
do: pulses, Doppler ABPI ± toe pressures; sensation.

numbers.meaning: mild compression ≤20 mmHg at the ankle
ABPI <0.5 urgent vascular referral; full assessment within 14 days.

recall.finish: document, refer for venous duplex/vascular service, give ischaemia/infection precautions.

partner.opening: Examine the lower legs of a 69-year-old patient with a right lower-leg ulcer.
partner.actorBrief: “This ulcer by my ankle has not healed.” Do not volunteer an ABPI result; one has not been done.

reveals.finding: Brown haemosiderin pigmentation, ankle oedema and varicosities bilaterally.

reveals.trigger: On ulcer examination (only provide the 3 × 2 cm size when examined or explicitly requested)
reveals.finding: Model shows shallow 3 × 2 cm right medial gaiter ulcer, irregular sloping edge, granulation and moderate serous exudate.

reveals.trigger: If asked about infection or systemic illness
reveals.finding: No fever, erythema spreading beyond the wound or purulent discharge.

reveals.trigger: On arterial examination (only provide the faint right posterior tibial pulse when examined or explicitly requested)
reveals.finding: Right foot warm, posterior tibial pulse faint, dorsalis pedis palpable; no rest pain.

reveals.trigger: If ABPI is requested (do not volunteer an ABPI result; one has not been done)

curveballs.prompt: After candidate’s compression plan: “Can you put the tight bandage on today?”
curveballs.safeAnswer: I would arrange formal arterial assessment before prescribing full therapeutic compression. If there is clinically important arterial disease, compression needs specialist assessment rather than routine application.

curveballs.prompt: Near the end: “What if my foot goes suddenly cold and very painful?”
curveballs.safeAnswer: That is an emergency suggesting acute limb ischaemia. They need immediate emergency assessment, not routine clinic follow-up. I would arrange urgent vascular escalation.
